correctness.rationale: PASS. Berger's Theorem 1.4 gives almost-everywhere convergence to \(N\) distinct basin measures; positivity of every basin weight follows from minimality of the finite small-scale emergence value. Proposition 1.3 then makes the two metric emergences equal. For the atomic empirical-limit law, the \(N-1\)-prototype distortion is bounded below by the pigeonhole principle plus the triangle inequality: two atoms share a center, and their weighted contribution is at least the smaller weight times their mutual distance. Choosing all atoms except the smaller-weight member of a pair attaining the minimum gives the matching upper bound. The strict \(<\varepsilon\) condition in the source definition correctly keeps the emergence equal to \(N\) at \(\varepsilon=\Delta\). No computation or unproved limiting interchange is used.

value.rationale: PASS. Finite second emergence tells how many asymptotic statistics survive at arbitrarily fine resolution but does not give the finite resolution at which one of them can first be discarded. The exact breakpoint \(\Delta\) combines basin mass and Wasserstein separation into a canonical robustness margin. It is invariantly defined by the empirical-limit law, applies without measure invariance, and is the complete answer to the first nontrivial compression problem from \(N\) to at most \(N-1\), rather than an arbitrary parameter slice or numerical recomputation.
